title: The Himalayas
hookLine: Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim, Nepal: Vajrayana in the mountains

lines: ACROSS THE ROOF OF THE WORLD.
cards: The Tiger's Nest. That's what people call a monastery that clings to a cliff face, white walls and golden roofs, hanging over a drop so steep that clouds drift below it. Pilgrims climb a long, narrow path to reach it.
And it isn't in Tibet. It's in Bhutan. Tradition says Padmasambhava, a teacher Tibetan tradition honors as a second Buddha, flew there on the back of a tigress and meditated in a cave in the rock.
Tibet gave the Vajrayana much of its shape, but this path has long lived across the whole roof of the world.

teach.b: Bhutan is a small kingdom east of Nepal where the Vajrayana runs through public life.
Its great fortress-monasteries, called dzongs, often hold government offices on one side of the courtyard and monks on the other.

The Drukpa Kagyu lineage is at the heart of its religious life, and festivals there fill courtyards with masked dancers. Ladakh is a high, dry land in India's far north, all brown mountains and blue sky.

Monasteries such as Thiksey rise on hilltops above the villages, prayer flags snapping in the wind, and Ladakhi Buddhists keep traditions close to Tibet's, in their own language and with their own festivals.

Sikkim is a small Indian state on the slopes below Kangchenjunga, with green valleys and monasteries tucked into forest. Rumtek, near its capital, became a seat of the Karma Kagyu lineage after its teachers left Tibet.
In Nepal, in Kathmandu, the great white dome of Boudhanath stupa looks out over the city with painted eyes, and Tibetan, Sherpa and Nepali Buddhists walk around it, clockwise, turning prayer wheels.
Nepal also holds Lumbini, which Buddhists honor as the place where the Buddha was born. These places didn't simply borrow a religion. Each has its own lineages, saints and ways of practice.
And when Tibetan teachers went into exile, some found shelter in these same mountains, among people who already chanted the same mantras.

how: Vajrayana Buddhists in Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim and Nepal keep their own lineages, monasteries and festivals, and these regions also became homes for Tibetan teachers in exile.

games.q: you're a pilgrim in Bhutan, looking up at a monastery on a sheer cliff, clouds below it. what do you do?
o: climb the long, narrow path to reach it.
wait for a road to be built.
games.why: pilgrims climb to the Tiger's Nest on foot, to the cave where tradition says Padmasambhava meditated.

practice: Open a map, or picture one, find the long curve of the Himalayas, and place them one by one: Ladakh in the west, then Nepal, then Sikkim, then Bhutan, with Tibet to the north.

Linger on each name for a breath, and think of a monastery bell ringing there right now, someone turning a prayer wheel, someone climbing toward a cliff. Then set the map down and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The Himalayas. The mountains where the Vajrayana lives on in Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim and Nepal, each place with its own lineages and ways. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit himālaya: hima, snow, and ālaya, dwelling. The abode of snow.
